topics.title: Body Fluids: Jobs, Compartments, and Age
topics.summary: Your body is mostly water. How much there is, where it sits, and what is dissolved in it decide whether cells can do their job.
objectives: You can use the four nursing questions to organize any fluid problem.
You can name the five jobs of body fluid and give a bedside example of each.
You can name the fluid compartments and say where most body water lives.
You can define body fluid, solute, electrolyte, osmolality, and homeostasis in plain words.
You can explain why infants and older adults lose fluid balance more easily.
You can say what the nurse monitors for volume, concentration, and electrolytes.
topics.bigPicture:
Every cell in your client's body sits in water and is made mostly of water. Water carries oxygen and food to cells. It carries wastes away, keeps body temperature steady, and cushions organs. When the amount of fluid or its makeup drifts off, cells stop working well. Then organs stop working well.

The body works all day to keep fluid in balance. This steady state is called homeostasis. Usually it happens without anyone noticing. But clients who are very young, very old, sick, or unable to drink on their own can lose balance fast. Nurses are often the first to notice and the first to act.
recap: Body fluid is water plus dissolved substances (solutes). Electrolytes are the solutes that carry a charge.
Body fluid controls temperature, keeps cell shape, carries nutrients and wastes, cushions organs, and keeps fluids balanced.
Most body water is inside cells (ICF). The rest is outside cells (ECF).
ECF has three parts: interstitial (the largest), intravascular (blood, about 5 L), and transcellular (CSF, pleural, joint, eye fluid).
Balance means the right volume, the right concentration, and the right electrolyte levels. Daily gains should equal daily losses.
Body water drops with age: about 90% premature, 75% newborn, 60% adult, 45–50% older adult.
Infants lose fluid within hours. Older adults dehydrate quietly and may not feel thirsty.
Monitor volume with I&O, weight, and assessment; concentration with the IV fluid ordered; electrolytes with labs.

keyTerms.def: The body's steady, balanced inner state. The body keeps adjusting to stay there.
Water plus the substances dissolved in it.
Anything dissolved in a fluid, such as sodium, glucose, or protein.
A solute with an electric charge (an ion). Examples: sodium (Na⁺), potassium (K⁺), calcium (Ca²⁺), magnesium (Mg²⁺), bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻), phosphate (PO₄³⁻).
A cation is a positive ion, like Na⁺. An anion is a negative ion, like HCO₃⁻.
How concentrated a fluid is: how many particles are dissolved in a set amount of fluid.
Fluid inside the cells. Most body fluid is here, about two-thirds of body water.
All fluid outside the cells: interstitial, intravascular, and transcellular fluid. About one-third of body water.
Fluid in the spaces around and between cells. It is the largest part of the ECF. Edema fluid sits here.
Fluid inside blood vessels (plasma). An adult's total blood volume is about 5 L.
Small amounts of special fluid in body spaces: cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), pleural fluid, joint fluid, and eye fluid.
The movement of fluid between compartments, so cells get nutrients and get rid of wastes.
One of the tiny filtering units in the kidney. Older adults have fewer working nephrons.

sections.heading: How should I think about fluids?
sections.keyIdea: For any client, ask four questions: what is normal, what is abnormal, what do I see, and what do I do?
sections.body:
Fluids and electrolytes can feel like a pile of numbers. Your instructor gives you a simple way to sort it. For every client, ask the four questions in the steps below.

This semester you build question 1, what is normal. The specific imbalance conditions (pages 384–387 in your textbook) are NUR 112 material. If you know normal well, you will spot abnormal later.

Two things about body fluid matter. The amount of fluid affects how the body works. The makeup of the fluid, meaning what is dissolved in it, keeps cells working. Nurses watch both.
steps: What is normal? How fluids and electrolytes stay in balance.
What is abnormal? Too little fluid, too much fluid, or lab values outside the normal range.
What do I see? The client's signs and symptoms.
What do I do? Nursing actions and treatments.
sections.analogy: Think of body fluid like the water in a fish tank. Your cells are the fish. The fish need the right amount of water, and the water needs the right chemistry. A half-empty tank is a problem. A full tank that is too salty is also a problem.

sections.heading: What jobs do body fluids do?
sections.keyIdea: Body fluid controls temperature, keeps cell shape, carries supplies and wastes, cushions organs, and keeps fluids balanced.
sections.body:
Your slides list five jobs of body fluid. Learn one example of each. Exam questions often describe the job instead of naming it.

The last job is the big rule for this whole module. The fluid gained across the day must equal the fluid lost.

table.caption: The five jobs of body fluid
rows: Blood carries heat to the skin. Sweat evaporates and cools the skin.
A client with a fever sweats. Sweat cools them but costs them water.
Water inside cells keeps them plump and firm.
A grape is full of water. A raisin has lost it. Cells shrink when they lose water.
Plasma brings oxygen, glucose, and electrolytes to cells. It carries wastes to the kidneys and lungs.
The kidneys need enough fluid to flush wastes out in urine.
CSF cushions the brain. Joint fluid cushions knees. Amniotic fluid protects a fetus.
Fluid moves between compartments so each stays balanced.
Intake across the day matches output across the day.

check.q: A client sweats heavily with a fever. Which jobs of body fluid are at work, and what is the trade-off?
check.a: Temperature control (sweat cools the skin) and fluid balance. The trade-off: sweating spends water and electrolytes, so the client needs more intake. Track I&O, especially in older adults.

sections.heading: What is body fluid made of?
sections.keyIdea: Body fluid is water plus solutes; electrolytes are the charged solutes, with sodium mostly outside cells and potassium mostly inside.
sections.body:
Body fluid is water plus what is dissolved in it. The dissolved things are called solutes. Solutes that carry an electric charge are called electrolytes, or ions.

The small + or − sign shows the charge. Positive ions are cations. Negative ions are anions. Chloride (Cl⁻) shows up later as sodium's partner. Electrolytes let nerves send signals and muscles contract, including the heart. They also help control where water goes.

All body fluids hold electrolytes, but the amount depends on location. Sodium is the main electrolyte outside cells. Potassium is the main electrolyte inside cells. A balanced client has the three things in the bullets below.
bullets: The right volume: enough water overall, and enough in the blood vessels.
The right concentration (osmolality): the right number of particles dissolved in that water.
The right electrolyte levels: Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, and the others in their normal ranges.
sections.analogy: Think of lemonade. Volume is how many glasses you have. Concentration is how strong it tastes. You can have plenty of glasses that taste too strong, or the right taste but too few glasses. So normal concentration does not rule out a volume problem.

sections.heading: Where does body fluid live?
sections.keyIdea: Most body water is inside cells; outside cells, the largest share is interstitial fluid, not blood.
sections.body:
Body fluid sits in two main areas called compartments. Intracellular fluid (ICF) is inside the cells. It holds most body fluid: about 40% of body weight, or two-thirds of body water.

Extracellular fluid (ECF) is outside the cells. It is about 20% of body weight, or one-third of body water. Your slides say these percents are for reference, not memorizing. Do know that more fluid is inside cells than outside.

The ECF has three parts, shown in the table. Interstitial fluid is the biggest part. Blood is only about 5 L in an adult.

table.caption: Body fluid compartments
rows: Holds most body fluid (about 40% of body weight)
About 20% of body weight; three parts below
Largest part of the ECF; where edema fluid collects
Blood volume about 5 L in an adult
CSF, pleural, joint, and eye fluid

sections.analogy: Picture a town. Water inside the houses is the ICF, and most of the town's water is there. Water in the yards and soil is the interstitial fluid. Water in the pipes is the blood. A few special tanks, like a pool, are the transcellular fluid.

check.q: A provider drains fluid from around a client's lung. Which compartment did that fluid come from?
check.a: Transcellular fluid, a small part of the ECF. Pleural fluid is a special fluid in a body space.

sections.heading: How does fluid reach the cells?
sections.keyIdea: Compartments are linked by thin membranes, and cells depend on fluid moving between them.
sections.body:
The compartments are not sealed boxes. Thin walls separate them: the cell membrane around each cell and the capillary wall around the tiniest blood vessels. Cells depend on fluid moving between these spaces.

Oxygen and nutrients travel from the blood, through the interstitial fluid, into the cell. Wastes travel the other way. This movement is called distribution. It is one of three processes that keep balance: intake and absorption, distribution, and output.

Two practical points follow. When a client bleeds, the blood vessels empty first. The interstitial space is the nearest reserve to refill them. Also, every blood lab you draw describes the fluid outside cells, not inside.
sections.example: At the bedside: Ms. R, 45, gets IV fluid into a vein in her arm. Where does it go first? Into the blood vessels, because it went straight into a vein. From there, some stays in the vessels, some moves to the interstitial space, and some may enter cells. Where it ends up depends on the type of fluid. You will learn the types in the IV solutions lesson.

sections.heading: How does body water change with age?
sections.keyIdea: Body water falls from about 90% in a premature infant to 45–50% in an older adult.
sections.body:
The share of the body that is water changes a lot with age, as the table shows.

Why do older adults have less water? Muscle holds a lot of water. Fat holds very little. People usually lose muscle as they age. Less muscle means less total body water and a smaller reserve. So the same loss hurts an older adult more.

check.q: Why might a muscular 30-year-old handle a day of low intake better than a frail 85-year-old?
check.a: The younger adult has more muscle, so more body water (about 60% vs 45–50%). They also have normal thirst and full kidney reserve. The older adult has less water, weaker thirst, and fewer working nephrons.

sections.heading: Why are infants and older adults at risk?
sections.keyIdea: Infants lose fluid within hours; older adults dehydrate without feeling thirsty, so the nurse plans fluids instead of waiting.
sections.body:
Infants are at higher risk for fluid loss. They can only show thirst by crying, and they depend on caregivers for every drink. Their skin and lung surface is large for their size, so they lose fluid fast through skin and breath. Their kidneys are immature and cannot save water well.

Older adults are at higher risk for dehydration. Their thirst sense is weaker. They have less muscle, so less water. Their kidneys have fewer working nephrons, so they adjust slowly. Dehydration can happen with no thirst at all.

Skin turgor (how fast pinched skin flattens) is not reliable in older adults. Trust intake, urine amount and color, weight, and mental status instead.
bullets: Offer fluids on a schedule. Do not wait for the client to ask.
Keep fluids within reach. After a stroke, place them on the client's strong side.
Offer drinks the client likes, and respect cultural choices within a safe plan.
Teach infant caregivers to offer fluids often, count wet diapers, and call early.
Speak up early if an older adult's NPO time (nothing by mouth) runs long.
sections.example: At the bedside: Mr. T, 86, lives in long-term care. He says, “I'm not thirsty,” and has barely touched his water. Should you wait until he asks? No. His weak thirst sense means “not thirsty” does not mean “enough fluid.” You offer his favorite drinks on a schedule and track his I&O and urine.

sections.heading: What does the nurse monitor?
sections.keyIdea: Check volume with I&O, weight, and assessment; concentration with the IV fluid type; electrolytes with lab values.
sections.body:
Nurses protect balance by watching three areas. Each one matches a part of “balance,” as the table shows. Your instructor's key rule: balance happens when intake matches output, fluid is absorbed, and fluid moves correctly in the body.

A balanced client shows intake about equal to output, a stable weight, enough urine, and labs in normal range. Assistive personnel (AP) can offer fluids, measure and record I&O, and weigh clients. The RN assesses, interprets the numbers, teaches, and evaluates.

table.caption: What the nurse monitors
rows: Intake and output (I&O), daily weight, physical assessment
The type of IV fluid ordered

sections.example: At the bedside: Mrs. L, 72, is admitted after two days of vomiting. For volume, you start strict I&O and assess her. For concentration, you check which IV fluid is ordered and what it will do. For electrolytes, you review her labs and report abnormal values. You have covered all three parts of balance.

sections.heading: Common traps: look-alikes to tell apart
sections.keyIdea: Most wrong answers swap a compartment, confuse volume with concentration, or trust thirst in an older adult.
sections.body: These pairs sound alike but mean different things. Read each answer choice slowly and match it to the right column.

table.caption: Look-alikes and how to tell them apart
rows: Most body water vs largest part of the ECF
Most body water is inside cells (ICF). The largest part of the ECF is interstitial fluid.
Interstitial is between cells. Intravascular is inside vessels (blood, about 5 L).
Transcellular is special fluid in spaces: CSF, pleural, joint, eye. Interstitial bathes all cells.
Volume is how much fluid. Concentration is how many particles. One can be normal while the other is off.
In an older adult, these are not the same. Check intake, urine, and weight.
Infant risk vs older adult risk
Infants lose fluid fast. Older adults have small reserves and weak thirst.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Questions describe a client and ask you to spot who is most at risk or which compartment is involved.
sections.body: Common question patterns:
bullets: Which client is at highest risk for fluid loss?
Which compartment holds this fluid? Transcellular is a favorite.
What do you teach about an older adult who “never asks for water”?
Which task can go to assistive personnel?
steps: Read the stem: “The nurse is caring for four clients. Which client is at highest risk for a rapid fluid imbalance?” A) 30-year-old with a sprained ankle. B) 70-year-old after knee surgery, drinking well. C) 6-month-old vomiting for 12 hours. D) 45-year-old with a mild cold.
What is it really asking? Who will lose balance fastest?
Key cues: “6-month-old” and “vomiting” are an ongoing loss in a small body.
Why the others are wrong: A and D have no real fluid loss. B is older, but she is drinking well with no ongoing loss.
The answer: C. Infants have a large surface area, immature kidneys, and no words for thirst. Their balance can change within hours.

check.q: Reusable strategy: what two cues point to the highest fluid risk?
check.a: Age at the extremes (infant or older adult) plus an ongoing loss (vomiting, diarrhea, fever, bleeding). The smaller the client and the bigger the loss, the faster the imbalance.

sections.heading: Worked case: an older adult in heat
sections.keyIdea: Weak thirst plus a hot day plus low intake equals silent dehydration; plan and measure fluids.
sections.body: Mrs. A, 84, lives in an assisted living home. It is a hot week. She had a stroke and has weak use of her left hand. Her water cup sits on her left side. She says she is not thirsty. Her urine is dark and small in amount.
steps: What is normal? Intake should about equal output, with steady weight and enough urine.
What is abnormal? Low intake, dark scant urine, and heat losses through sweat.
Why is she at risk? Weak thirst, less muscle water, and fewer working nephrons.
First fix the barrier: move the cup to her right, stronger side.
Then plan: offer drinks she likes on a schedule, track I&O and urine color, and weigh her.
Report: tell the provider if intake stays low or urine drops.

check.q: An AP says, “She told me she's not thirsty, so I didn't push it.” What do you teach?
check.a: Older adults have a weak thirst sense, so “not thirsty” does not mean hydrated. Offer fluids on a schedule, keep them on her strong side, and record every amount.

pearls: Most body fluid is intracellular. Within the ECF, the largest part is interstitial, not intravascular. Questions love to swap these.
Know the order: premature 90%, newborn 75%, adult 60%, older adult 45–50% water.
“Not thirsty” is not “well hydrated” in an older adult. Offer fluids on a schedule.
Infant fluid risk points to large surface area, immature kidneys, and total dependence on caregivers.
Balance means right volume, right concentration, and right electrolytes. One can be off while the others look normal.
Under a warmer or with fever, unseen losses climb. Daily weights catch what I&O misses.
redFlags: An infant feeding poorly or losing fluid (vomiting, diarrhea, few wet diapers) needs same-day evaluation. Assess hydration and report promptly.
An older adult with poor intake who says they are not thirsty: offer fluids, monitor I&O, and report falling urine output.
Rapid bleeding threatens circulation fast, because blood vessels hold only about 5 L.

checks.q: A student says, “Most of the body's water is in the bloodstream.” How do you correct this?
checks.a: Most body water is inside cells (ICF, about two-thirds). Blood (about 5 L) is only part of the ECF, and interstitial fluid is the largest part of the ECF.

checks.q: Which client is at highest risk for rapid fluid loss: a 25-year-old athlete, a 50-year-old office worker, or a premature infant?
checks.a: The premature infant. About 90% water, large surface area for size, immature kidneys, and full dependence on caregivers.

checks.q: An 80-year-old's daughter says, “Mom never asks for water, so she must be fine.” What do you teach?
checks.a: Older adults have a weak thirst sense and can dehydrate without feeling thirsty. Offer fluids on a schedule, keep them in sight, and watch her urine.

checks.q: You want to check a client's fluid concentration. Which monitoring area is this, and what do you look at?
checks.a: Concentration (osmolality). Your slides tie it to the type of IV fluid ordered, because different fluids change concentration differently.

topics.title: How Fluid Moves: Filtration, Osmosis, Diffusion, Pumps
topics.summary: Pressure pushes fluid, water follows sodium, particles spread out, and energy pumps particles uphill. These four ideas explain how fluid reaches every cell.
objectives: You can name the four ways fluid and particles move between compartments.
You can explain filtration at the capillary and three reasons edema forms.
You can predict which way water moves by osmosis and tell osmosis from diffusion.
You can explain the sodium-potassium pump and why it needs energy (ATP).
You can predict what isotonic, hypotonic, and hypertonic fluids do to cells.
topics.bigPicture:
Fluid that enters the body cannot just sit still. Oxygen and food must get from the blood to the cells. Wastes must get back to the blood. Water must keep moving so the inside and outside of cells stay at the same strength. This movement between compartments is called distribution.

Four processes do this work: filtration, osmosis, diffusion, and active transport. Three are passive, meaning they need no energy. One is active, so the cell must spend energy. Once these click, edema, thirst, IV fluids, and many lab changes start to make sense.
recap: Filtration: pressure pushes fluid out of capillaries at the arterial end. Fluid returns at the venous end, pulled by albumin.
Edema forms when capillary pressure rises, albumin falls, or lymph drainage is lost.
Osmosis moves water toward the side with more solute. Water follows sodium.
Diffusion moves particles from high concentration to low concentration.
Only active transport needs ATP. The Na⁺/K⁺ pump moves sodium out and potassium in. Magnesium helps switch it on.
When many cells break down, potassium and phosphate spill into the blood.
Normal serum osmolality is 280–300 mOsm/kg. Rising osmolality pulls water from cells and triggers thirst and ADH.
Hypotonic fluid swells cells. Hypertonic fluid shrinks cells. Isotonic fluid causes no major shift.

keyTerms.def: Movement of fluids and electrolytes between compartments: inside cells, between cells, and inside vessels.
A wall that lets some things through, like water, but blocks others, like large proteins. Cell membranes and capillary walls are semipermeable.
A difference in concentration between two areas. High to low is “downhill.” Low to high is “uphill.”
Fluid pushed out of capillaries into tissues by pressure.
The pushing force of fluid against its container, like blood pushing on a capillary wall. The heartbeat creates most of it.
The water-pulling force of proteins in the blood, mainly albumin. It draws fluid back into vessels.
Water moving across a semipermeable membrane toward the side with more dissolved particles.
Particles moving from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration.
Moving particles uphill, from low to high concentration. It needs energy (ATP).
Adenosine triphosphate: the cell's energy supply.
A pump in every cell membrane. It moves sodium out of the cell and potassium into the cell, using ATP.
How many particles are dissolved in a fluid. Normal serum osmolality is 280–300 mOsm/kg.
How a fluid's concentration compares with blood and cells. It tells you which way water will move.
Swelling from extra fluid in the interstitial space (the tissues).
Red blood cells breaking open. It releases the potassium inside them.

sections.heading: What is distribution?
sections.keyIdea: Fluid and particles cross thin membranes between compartments by four processes; only one needs energy.
sections.body:
Distribution is fluid moving between compartments. Fluid inside cells is the ICF. Fluid outside cells is the ECF, which includes the space between cells and the bloodstream.

A semipermeable membrane separates each compartment. The cell membrane separates the inside of the cell from the fluid around it. The capillary wall separates blood from tissue. Some things pass easily, and some do not.

Things naturally move “downhill,” from where there is more to where there is less. They stop when both sides are even. Moving “uphill” takes energy. To name a process, ask three things. What moves? Which way? Does it cost energy?

table.caption: The four processes at a glance

sections.heading: How does filtration push fluid out?
sections.keyIdea: Pressure pushes fluid out at the arterial end of a capillary; albumin pulls it back in at the venous end.
sections.body:
Filtration moves fluid between blood vessels and tissues. It happens in capillaries, the tiny vessels where blood meets tissue.

Each heartbeat creates pressure in the vessels, called hydrostatic pressure. At the arterial end of a capillary, pressure is higher. It pushes fluid out into the tissues. That fluid carries oxygen and nutrients to cells.

At the venous end, pressure has dropped. Now fluid moves back in. Large proteins, mainly albumin, stay inside the vessel because they are too big to leak out. They pull water back. This pull is oncotic pressure. The returning fluid carries wastes like carbon dioxide. Lymph vessels pick up the small amount left over and return it to the blood.
sections.analogy: Think of a soaker hose with tiny holes. Water pressure pushes water out the holes to soak the soil. Near the end, pressure is low. Now picture sponges inside the hose (albumin) soaking water back in. Push out at the start, pull back in at the end.

check.q: At which end of the capillary does pressure push fluid out into the tissues?
check.a: The arterial end, where hydrostatic pressure is higher. Fluid returns at the venous end, pulled by albumin's oncotic pressure.

sections.heading: Why does edema form?
sections.keyIdea: Edema forms when capillary pressure rises, albumin falls, or lymph drainage is lost.
sections.body:
Edema is extra fluid stuck in the tissues. It forms when the push-and-pull of filtration gets out of balance. There are three main causes, listed below.

Edema collects where capillary pressure is highest. In a client who walks, that is the feet and legs. In a bedbound client, check the sacrum (lower back). Raising swollen legs lowers their capillary pressure. Drinking less does not fix this kind of swelling.

If fluid builds up in the lungs, breathing becomes the priority. Swollen skin also breaks down easily. Reposition often, do not massage swollen areas, and report redness.
bullets: Pressure goes up: more push forces more fluid into the tissues.
Albumin goes down: a weak “magnet” cannot pull fluid back into vessels.
Lymph drainage is lost: leftover fluid is not carried away, such as after lymph nodes are removed. Protect that arm from pressure and injury.
sections.example: At the bedside: Mrs. G, 58, has a very low albumin after weeks of poor eating. Her legs and feet are swollen. Pressure still pushes fluid out at the arterial end. But with little albumin, there is not enough pull to bring it back. More protein in her diet treats the cause. When her albumin rises and the swelling shrinks, the pull is working again.

sections.heading: Osmosis: why does water follow sodium?
sections.keyIdea: In osmosis, only water moves, and it moves toward the side with more dissolved particles.
sections.body:
Osmosis is water moving across a semipermeable membrane. Only water moves. The particles stay put because they cannot cross, or cross slowly.

Your slides say water moves “from LOW concentration to HIGH concentration.” Concentration here means dissolved particles. So water leaves the dilute side and moves to the crowded side. It keeps moving until both sides match.

Sodium is the main particle that pulls water. That is why we say water follows sodium. Cutting sodium is how you cut retained fluid. If the ECF gets more concentrated, water leaves the cells. If the ECF gets more dilute, water enters the cells. No ATP is needed.
sections.analogy: Put a cucumber in salty brine. Over time the brine pulls water out, and the cucumber shrinks into a pickle. The water moved toward the salt.
sections.example: At the bedside: Mr. D, 40, eats a big bag of salty chips. Sodium enters his blood, so his ECF gets more concentrated. Water moves out of his cells toward the salty ECF. The rise in concentration makes him thirsty, so he drinks. The water brings his ECF back to normal.

check.q: The fluid outside a cell becomes more concentrated than the fluid inside. Which way does water move?
check.a: Out of the cell, toward the more concentrated ECF. The cell shrinks.

sections.heading: Diffusion: how do particles spread out?
sections.keyIdea: In diffusion, particles move from where there are many to where there are few, with no energy.
sections.body:
Diffusion is particles moving across a membrane from high concentration to low. They spread out until the space is even. No energy is needed.

Gas exchange is the classic example. Oxygen is high in the lungs' air sacs and low in the blood, so it diffuses into the blood. In the tissues, oxygen is high in blood and low in busy cells, so it moves into cells. Carbon dioxide moves the opposite way, down its own gradient. Giving extra oxygen makes the oxygen gradient steeper.

The bullets pair diffusion with osmosis. Notice that particles and water move in opposite directions. Both move toward the same goal: equal concentration.
bullets: High solute means less water.
Low solute means more water.
Solute moves from high to low (diffusion).
Water moves toward high solute (osmosis).

table.caption: Osmosis vs diffusion
rows: Water leaving cells when the ECF is salty
Oxygen moving from blood into cells

sections.analogy: Drop a tea bag into hot water and do not stir. The dark tea slowly spreads from the bag into the clear water. Soon the whole cup is the same color.

sections.heading: Active transport: what does the pump do?
sections.keyIdea: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump uses ATP to push sodium out and pull potassium in, keeping potassium inside cells.
sections.body:
Sometimes the body must keep particles where they are already crowded. That means moving them uphill, from low to high. This needs energy, called ATP.

The best example is the sodium-potassium pump in every cell membrane. It moves sodium out of the cell and potassium in. That keeps sodium high outside cells and potassium high inside. The difference lets nerves fire and muscles contract, including the heart. Magnesium helps switch the pump on.

Labs measure the ECF only. So when many cells break open, their potassium and phosphate spill into the blood. The level rises even though intake did not change.
bullets: Low magnesium and low potassium together: replace magnesium first, so the pump can hold potassium.
Major tissue injury or chemotherapy can break many cells. Watch for rising potassium, check the heart rhythm, and report.
A hemolyzed blood sample can show a falsely high potassium, because broken red cells released it.
Never give potassium by IV push. It is diluted and given on a pump.
sections.analogy: Riding a bike downhill takes no effort, like diffusion and osmosis. Riding uphill takes work. That is active transport, and the cell pedals with ATP.

check.q: Which of the four processes is the only one that needs ATP?
check.a: Active transport, because it moves particles uphill. Example: the Na⁺/K⁺ pump moving sodium out and potassium in.

sections.heading: What do isotonic, hypotonic, and hypertonic mean?
sections.keyIdea: Compare a fluid with blood: dilute fluid swells cells, concentrated fluid shrinks them, matching fluid leaves them alone.
sections.body:
Osmolality is how concentrated a fluid is. Normal serum osmolality is 280–300 mOsm/kg. Sodium adds the most to it. When osmolality rises, water leaves cells. The body triggers thirst and releases antidiuretic hormone (ADH) so the kidneys save water.

Tonicity compares a fluid, such as an IV bag, with blood and cells. It tells you which way water will move. See the table.

Only 0.9% sodium chloride is hung with a blood transfusion. A dilute fluid would make the red cells swell and burst. In the same way, saline protects exposed tissue, while plain water makes cells swell.

table.caption: Tonicity: which way does water move?

sections.analogy: Picture red blood cells as grapes. In a matching fluid, they stay plump. In a dilute fluid, water rushes in and they swell. In a salty fluid, water is pulled out and they shrivel like raisins.
sections.example: At the bedside: Too much plain water dilutes the ECF and swells cells. This can happen with infant formula mixed with extra water. It can happen when heavy sweat is replaced with plain water alone. New confusion during a free-water IV infusion is a warning sign. Slow it and report.

sections.heading: How do I predict where fluid goes?
sections.keyIdea: Check pressure, albumin, sodium, and particle movement, then predict where the water ends up.
sections.body: In a real client, all four processes run at once. Use these steps whenever you need to predict where fluid will go.
steps: Pressure: is pressure in the vessels up? More pressure pushes more fluid into tissues.
Albumin: is it low? Low albumin means less pull back into vessels.
Sodium: is the ECF concentrated or dilute? Water moves toward the concentrated side.
Particles: are they spreading high to low, or is the cell spending energy to hold them?
Predict: will the water end up in the vessels, the tissues, or the cells?
sections.example: At the bedside: Mr. K, 66, gets a liter of isotonic IV fluid. Its strength matches his blood, so osmosis causes no major shift into cells. The added volume raises vessel pressure a little. So filtration moves some fluid into his tissues. Prediction: the fluid expands his ECF, both vessels and tissues, but not his cells. It may also dilute his hematocrit.

sections.heading: Common traps: look-alikes to tell apart
sections.keyIdea: Most errors mix up what moves (water or particles) or which way it goes.
sections.body: These pairs trip up many students. Use the table to sort them out.

table.caption: Look-alikes and how to tell them apart
rows: Osmosis moves water toward more solute. Diffusion moves particles from high to low.
Filtration is driven by pressure. Osmosis is driven by particle concentration.
Hydrostatic pushes fluid out of vessels. Oncotic (albumin) pulls fluid back in.
Hypotonic (dilute) swells cells. Hypertonic (concentrated) shrinks cells.
Filtration, osmosis, and diffusion are free. Only active transport uses ATP.
True high K⁺ vs false high K⁺
Cell breakdown in the body raises it truly. A hemolyzed sample raises it falsely.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Questions describe a fluid shift and ask you to name the process or predict what cells do.
sections.body: Common question patterns:
bullets: Name the process from a description: what moves, which way, and is energy used?
Predict what a fluid does to cells: swell, shrink, or stay the same.
Explain edema from low albumin or high pressure, then pick the right action.
Explain a lab change, such as high potassium after cell breakdown.
steps: Read the stem: “A client's albumin is 2.2 g/dL. The client has ankle edema and a blood pressure of 88/50. Which finding should the nurse address first?” A) Ankle edema. B) Low blood pressure. C) Dry skin. D) Poor appetite.
What is it really asking? Which effect of low albumin threatens the client most?
Key cues: low albumin means weak pull, so fluid leaves the vessels. BP 88/50 means poor blood flow to organs.
Why the others are wrong: Edema is uncomfortable but not the top threat. Dry skin and poor appetite matter later.
The answer: B. Falling blood pressure threatens perfusion, meaning blood flow to the organs, so it comes first.

check.q: Reusable strategy: when one cause creates many findings, which do you treat first?
check.a: The finding that threatens breathing or circulation. Name the process, then rank its effects by danger.

sections.heading: Worked case: confusion during an IV
sections.keyIdea: A dilute ECF drives water into cells; new confusion means slow the fluid and report.
sections.body: Mr. B, 70, is getting D5W. Once the sugar is used, it acts like plain water. Two hours in, he is newly confused and has a headache. His morning sodium was low-normal.
steps: What moved? Extra free water made his ECF more dilute.
Which process? Osmosis. Water moves toward the side with more solute, which is now inside his cells.
What does that do? His cells swell, including brain cells. That explains the confusion and headache.
What do I do? Slow the infusion, assess him, and report to the provider right away.
What do I watch? Mental status, sodium results, and I&O.

check.q: Would a hypertonic fluid cause the same problem? Why or why not?
check.a: No. A hypertonic fluid pulls water out of cells, so cells shrink. Mr. B's cells swelled because his ECF became dilute (hypotonic).

mnemonics.name: Push, Follow, Spread, Pump
mnemonics.text: Filtration pushes. Water follows sodium (osmosis). Particles spread (diffusion). The pump uses ATP (active transport).

pearls: Osmosis moves water; diffusion moves particles. An answer saying “osmosis moves sodium” is wrong.
Water moves toward the side with more solute. “Water follows sodium” is the shortcut.
Only active transport needs ATP. The Na⁺/K⁺ pump moves sodium out and potassium in.
Low albumin causes edema, ascites, low blood pressure, and poor wound healing.
Serum lab values describe the ECF only. Inside-cell levels are not measured directly.
Hypotonic swells cells, hypertonic shrinks them, isotonic causes no major shift.
redFlags: New crackles or shortness of breath during IV fluids: slow the infusion, raise the head of the bed, then notify the provider.
Rising potassium after major tissue injury: check the heart rhythm and report promptly.
New confusion during a free-water infusion: slow it and report, because cells may be swelling.

checks.q: A client's sodium rises after a very salty meal. Where does water move, and by which process?
checks.a: Out of the cells into the ECF, by osmosis. The higher osmolality also triggers thirst and ADH.

checks.q: Which process delivers oxygen and nutrients to tissues by pushing fluid out of the capillary?
checks.a: Filtration, driven by hydrostatic pressure at the arterial end.

checks.q: A cell sits in a fluid more dilute than its inside. What happens?
checks.a: Water moves into the cell by osmosis, so it swells. The fluid is hypotonic.

checks.q: Potassium is mostly inside cells and sodium mostly outside. What keeps it that way?
checks.a: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump (active transport). It moves sodium out and potassium in and costs ATP.

checks.q: A client's lab shows high potassium, but the lab notes the sample was hemolyzed. What does that suggest?
checks.a: The result may be falsely high. Broken red cells in the tube released their potassium. Report it so the sample can be redrawn.

topics.title: Intake, Absorption, Output, and Fluid Hormones
topics.summary: What goes in must roughly equal what comes out. Learn the routes, the daily numbers, the 0.5 mL/kg/hr urine rule, and three hormones that guide the kidneys.
objectives: You can list the routes of intake and record every source on the I&O.
You can explain thirst, absorption, and why unabsorbed fluid leaves in stool.
You can tell sensible losses from insensible losses.
You can calculate minimum urine output using 0.5 mL/kg/hr.
You can explain how aldosterone, ANF, and ADH change urine output.
You can decide what to delegate and what to report.
topics.bigPicture:
The body keeps balance with three processes. Intake and absorption bring fluid in. Distribution moves it around. Output sends it out. Balance needs all three.

Balance is always changing. Output goes on all the time, even during sleep. Intake changes through the day. Fluid shifts fast with fever, vomiting, or bleeding. For nurses, this is daily work. You measure intake and output (I&O), check whether urine is enough, and notice when losses outrun intake.
recap: Balance means intake about equals output. Output never stops, even with no intake.
Record ALL intake: oral, tube feedings and flushes, IV fluids, IV medications, and irrigations.
Thirst is triggered by rising osmolality, dry mouth, and falling blood volume.
Unabsorbed fluid leaves in stool. IV fluid skips absorption and enters the blood immediately.
Minimum urine output is 0.5 mL/kg/hr. Obligatory urine is 400–600 mL a day.
Sensible losses are measured and recorded. Insensible losses (skin, lungs) are not, but still count.
Aldosterone keeps sodium and water. ANF releases sodium and water. ADH keeps water only.
AP measure and record. The RN interprets the numbers and decides what to do.

keyTerms.def: All fluid entering the body: drinks, food, IV fluids, tube feedings, and other routes.
Fluid and electrolytes moving from the GI tract into the bloodstream.
All fluid leaving the body: urine, stool, sweat, breath, and abnormal losses.
Fluid loss you can measure, such as urine, stool, vomit, and drain output.
Fluid loss you cannot measure: evaporation from the skin and water vapor from the lungs.
The minimum urine, 400–600 mL a day, the body must make to clear wastes.
Fluid given slowly into the tissue under the skin (subcutaneous).
Into the bone marrow. Used for fluids when a vein cannot be reached.
An abnormal passage between two body parts, or between an organ and the skin, that can drain fluid.
An adrenal gland hormone. It makes the kidneys keep sodium and water and let potassium go, raising blood volume.
A hormone from the heart's upper chambers (atria). It opposes aldosterone, so the kidneys release sodium and water.
A pituitary gland hormone. It makes the kidneys keep water only, so urine becomes less and darker.
A urine test of how concentrated urine is. It rises when the kidneys are saving water.

sections.heading: How does the body stay in balance?
sections.keyIdea: Balance happens when intake about equals output, fluid is absorbed, and fluid moves correctly.
sections.body:
Think of fluid balance as money in a bank account. Intake is a deposit. Output is a withdrawal. Balance means deposits keep up with withdrawals.

Some withdrawals are automatic. Skin, lungs, and the minimum urine lose water every day, even if you drink nothing. Vomiting, bleeding, and drains are surprise withdrawals that can empty the account fast.

The body keeps adjusting to stay in balance. The kidneys make more urine when there is extra fluid and less when fluid is short. Hormones tell them what to keep.
bullets: Intake and absorption: what comes in and reaches the blood.
Distribution: where fluid moves between compartments.
Output: what leaves the body.

sections.heading: How does fluid get in?
sections.keyIdea: Drinking and eating are the main route, but every source of fluid goes on the I&O record.
sections.body:
Intake is all the fluid entering the body. The most common route is by mouth, through drinks and food. Food counts, because fruit, soup, and vegetables are mostly water. When a client cannot take enough by mouth, other routes help. See the table.

If the gut is not absorbing well, choose a route that skips the GI tract. That means IV, subcutaneous, or intraosseous. On the I&O record, count every source: oral fluids, tube feedings and water flushes, IV fluids, IV medications, and irrigations. Measure; do not estimate.

table.caption: Routes of intake
rows: Drinks and food. The most common route.
Fluid into a vein. It enters the blood immediately.
Fluid or formula through a tube into the stomach or intestine.
Fluid placed in the rectum or another cavity; some may be absorbed.
Fluid infused slowly under the skin.
Fluid into the bone marrow, when a vein cannot be reached.

check.q: A client gets tube feedings, water flushes, and an IV antibiotic. What goes on the intake record?
check.a: All of it: the formula, the flushes, and the IV medication volume, plus any IV fluids and oral intake.

sections.heading: What makes a person thirsty?
sections.keyIdea: Thirst is triggered by concentrated blood, dry mouth, and low blood volume, but it only works if the client can act.
sections.body:
Thirst is the body's signal to drink. The thirst center sits in the brain (hypothalamus). The steps show how it works.

Thirst only helps if the client can feel it and act on it. Older adults have a weak thirst sense. Infants can only cry. Confused or weak clients may not ask. For these clients, schedule fluids and measure them. For older adults who wake at night to urinate, give more fluids earlier in the day instead of cutting the total.
bullets: Rising fluid concentration (osmolality).
Dry mouth.
Falling blood volume.
steps: The body loses water, for example by sweating on a hot day.
The blood gets more concentrated, and the mouth feels dry.
Thirst is triggered.
The person drinks, the blood is diluted, and osmolality returns to normal.
sections.example: At the bedside: Mrs. P, 88, has a weak thirst sense and needs help to reach her cup. You cannot rely on her thirst. You offer fluids on a schedule, keep them within reach, and record each amount.

sections.heading: What is absorption?
sections.keyIdea: Fluid only counts once it is absorbed; what rushes through the bowel leaves in the stool.
sections.body:
A glass of water does not help cells until it reaches the blood. Absorption is fluid and electrolytes moving from the GI tract into the bloodstream. It happens mainly in the intestines.

IV fluid skips this step. It enters the blood immediately, which is why it acts faster than oral fluid. If fluid is not absorbed, it stays in the GI tract and leaves in stool. So a client can drink plenty and still come up short.
sections.example: At the bedside: Mr. S, 35, has had watery diarrhea for two days. He drinks about 2 L a day. Is he balanced? Not necessarily. Fluid moves through his bowel so fast that much is not absorbed. You measure his liquid stools, record them as output, and report the diarrhea.

check.q: Why does IV fluid change blood volume faster than the same amount taken by mouth?
check.a: IV fluid enters the blood immediately. Oral fluid must first be absorbed from the GI tract.

sections.heading: How does fluid leave the body?
sections.keyIdea: Urine is the main output; vomiting, bleeding, drains, and wounds are abnormal losses that shift balance fast.
sections.body:
Output is how fluid leaves. The normal routes are urine, stool, skin, and lungs. Urine is the biggest. The table shows daily amounts for a healthy adult. Intake and output are about equal. Drinking supplies only about half of daily water. Food and metabolism supply the rest.

Abnormal losses are vomiting, bleeding, drainage tubes or fistulas, and open wounds. Measure and record every abnormal loss. Report sharp increases. If vital signs are also unstable, escalate right away. Do not just document it.

table.caption: Daily intake and output for an adult (about)

sections.heading: How do I check urine output?
sections.keyIdea: Minimum urine output is 0.5 mL per kg per hour; always convert pounds to kilograms first.
sections.body:
Two numbers matter most. First, the body must make 400–600 mL of urine a day to clear wastes. This obligatory loss goes on even with no intake. Urine below it means wastes are not being cleared.

Second, your instructor says KNOW THIS: minimum urine output is 0.5 mL/kg/hr. Judge each client by their own weight. Balanced totals can still hide low urine.

If output is low, check the catheter for kinks and the bladder for fullness. Then report. AP can measure and record urine. Give them a clear number that means “tell me right away.”
steps: Get the weight in kilograms. If it is in pounds, divide by 2.2.
Multiply kg by 0.5. That is the minimum mL per hour.
Multiply by the number of hours you are checking.
Compare with the actual urine. If it is less, assess and report.
sections.example: At the bedside: Mr. A weighs 154 lb. 154 ÷ 2.2 = 70 kg. 70 × 0.5 = 35 mL/hr. Over 8 hours, he needs at least 280 mL. He made 450 mL, so he is fine. Ms. B weighs 60 kg. She needs 30 mL/hr, or 120 mL in 4 hours. Her bag shows 75 mL. That is too low, so you check her catheter and report.

check.q: A client weighs 80 kg and makes 30 mL/hr. Is that enough?
check.a: No. 80 × 0.5 = 40 mL/hr minimum. 30 mL/hr is too low, so assess and report.

sections.heading: Sensible vs insensible: which losses count?
sections.keyIdea: If you can measure it, record it; skin and lung losses are real but never added to the I&O total.
sections.body:
Sensible losses can be measured: urine, stool, vomit, and wound or drain output. Insensible losses cannot be measured. Skin loses water by evaporation, which rises with fever, heat, and dry air. Lungs lose water vapor, which rises with fast or deep breathing. Together, skin and lungs lose about 700–800 mL a day. Infants lose even more this way, because their skin and lung surface is large for their size.

Insensible losses are not on the I&O, but they still affect hydration. So a “balanced” record can hide a deficit. Daily weights catch what I&O misses. Weigh on the same scale, at the same time, in the same clothing.

table.caption: Sensible vs insensible
rows: Urine, stool, vomit, blood loss, drain output
Skin evaporation, water vapor from lungs
Fever, heat, low humidity, fast or deep breathing

sections.example: At the bedside: Mrs. H, 70, has a temperature of 39 °C (102.2 °F) and breathes 28 times a minute. Her I&O shows 1,800 mL in and 1,700 mL out. She is probably not balanced. Fever and fast breathing raise losses the sheet cannot show. You encourage fluids as ordered and weigh her daily.

sections.heading: Which hormones control urine?
sections.keyIdea: Aldosterone keeps sodium and water, ANF releases them, and ADH keeps water only.
sections.body:
The kidneys control most fluid output. Three hormones tell them what to keep or release.

Aldosterone comes from the adrenal glands when blood volume is low. It tells the kidneys to keep sodium and water. Since water follows sodium, blood volume rises. Potassium is let go in the urine.

ANF comes from the heart's atria when they are stretched by too much volume. It opposes aldosterone, so sodium and water leave and urine increases. Natri means sodium; uretic means urine.

ADH comes from the pituitary gland when body fluids are concentrated. It keeps water only, so urine becomes less, darker, and higher in specific gravity. Large amounts of very dilute urine suggest ADH is missing.

table.caption: Hormones that change urine output
rows: Keeps sodium AND water; lets potassium go
Atria are stretched by high volume

sections.analogy: Aldosterone is the salt-and-water saver. ANF is the overflow valve that opens when the heart is too full. ADH is the faucet control that turns down water flow into urine when the body runs dry.
sections.example: At the bedside: Mr. J, a roofer, works all day in the heat and drinks little. His blood gets concentrated, so ADH rises. He makes small amounts of dark urine. That evening he drinks three big bottles of water. His blood volume is also low, so aldosterone helps him keep sodium and water. ADH falls, and he makes more pale urine.

sections.heading: Common traps: look-alikes to tell apart
sections.keyIdea: Watch for swapped hormones, unrecorded insensible losses, and urine totals not checked against weight.
sections.body: These look-alikes show up often in answer choices. Slow down and check each one.

table.caption: Look-alikes and how to tell them apart
rows: Aldosterone keeps sodium AND water. ADH keeps water ONLY.
Opposites. Aldosterone keeps sodium and water; ANF releases them.
Sensible is measured and recorded. Insensible (skin, lungs) is not recorded.
Obligatory loss vs minimum hourly urine
Obligatory is 400–600 mL a day. Minimum hourly is 0.5 mL/kg/hr.
With diarrhea, fluid taken in may leave in stool without being absorbed.
The 0.5 rule uses kg. Divide pounds by 2.2 first.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Expect urine output math, hormone matching, hidden insensible losses, and delegation of I&O tasks.
sections.body: Common question patterns:
bullets: Is this urine output enough? Do the weight-based math.
Which hormone explains these findings?
Why is a “balanced” I&O misleading in a client with fever?
What can AP do with I&O, and what must the RN do?
steps: Read the stem: “A client weighs 176 lb. Urine output for the last 4 hours is 120 mL. What should the nurse do?” A) Document it as normal. B) Assess the client and catheter, then report. C) Increase the IV rate. D) Recheck in 4 hours.
What is it really asking? Is 120 mL in 4 hours enough for this client?
Key cues: 176 lb ÷ 2.2 = 80 kg. 80 × 0.5 = 40 mL/hr. Over 4 hours, the minimum is 160 mL.
Why the others are wrong: A is wrong; 120 mL is below 160 mL. C changes treatment without an order. D delays care.
The answer: B. Output is low, so assess, check for kinks, and report.

check.q: Reusable strategy for urine output questions?
check.a: Convert to kg, multiply by 0.5 and by the hours, and compare. If low, assess first, then report. Never just document a low number.

sections.heading: Worked case: a fever and a full sheet
sections.keyIdea: A balanced I&O can hide a deficit when fever and fast breathing raise unseen losses.
sections.body: Mr. L, 76, weighs 70 kg. He has pneumonia, a fever of 38.9 °C, and breathes 26 times a minute. His 8-hour I&O shows 900 mL in and 850 mL out. He made 200 mL of dark urine.
steps: Check urine: 70 × 0.5 = 35 mL/hr. Over 8 hours, he needs 280 mL. 200 mL is too low.
Look for hidden losses: fever and fast breathing raise skin and lung losses not on the sheet.
Read the urine: dark, small amounts mean ADH is saving water.
Act: assess him, check any catheter, and report the low output.
Plan: encourage fluids as ordered, keep strict I&O, and weigh him daily.

check.q: The AP says, “His in and out are almost equal, so he's fine.” What do you explain?
check.a: The I&O does not show skin and lung losses, which are high with fever and fast breathing. His urine is below 0.5 mL/kg/hr. He likely has a deficit.

mnemonics.name: Aldo saves salt, ADH saves water, ANF lets go
mnemonics.text: Aldosterone keeps sodium and water. ADH keeps water only. ANF releases both.

pearls: KNOW: urine output of at least 0.5 mL/kg/hr. Convert pounds to kg first, then multiply by 0.5 and the hours.
Insensible losses are not on the I&O but still count. Fever and fast breathing raise them.
Urine is the main output, about 1,400–1,500 mL a day. Obligatory minimum is 400–600 mL a day.
ADH up means less, darker urine. ADH down means more, paler urine.
Unabsorbed fluid leaves in stool. Good intake does not guarantee balance with diarrhea.
Weigh on the same scale, at the same time, in the same clothing, or the change is not real data.
redFlags: Urine below 0.5 mL/kg/hr (under 35 mL/hr for a 70-kg adult): assess the client and catheter, then report.
Large abnormal losses (vomiting, bleeding, high drain output) with unstable vital signs: escalate right away.
An infant or older adult with poor intake: do not wait for thirst. Offer fluids, track I&O, and report low intake.
New crackles or shortness of breath during a fluid infusion in an older adult: this outranks routine site checks.

checks.q: A 110-lb client made 60 mL of urine in 4 hours. Is this enough?
checks.a: No. 110 ÷ 2.2 = 50 kg. 50 × 0.5 = 25 mL/hr, so 100 mL in 4 hours. 60 mL is low; assess and report.

checks.q: A client's blood becomes concentrated after a day without drinking. Which hormone rises, and what happens to urine?
checks.a: ADH rises. The kidneys keep water, so urine becomes less and more concentrated.

checks.q: The heart's atria are stretched by extra volume. Which hormone is released, and what does it do?
checks.a: ANF. It opposes aldosterone, so sodium and water leave and urine increases.

checks.q: Why is 400–600 mL of urine a day called an obligatory loss?
checks.a: The body must make at least that much urine to clear wastes, even with no intake.

checks.q: Name four abnormal routes of fluid loss.
checks.a: Vomiting, bleeding (hemorrhage), drainage tubes or fistulas, and open wounds.

checks.q: Which I&O tasks can go to AP?
checks.a: Measuring and recording intake and output, and weighing. The RN interprets the numbers, assesses, and decides what to do.

topics.title: IV Solutions: Crystalloids, Colloids, and Albumin
topics.summary: Every IV bag does a specific job. Small-particle crystalloids spread through the ECF. Large-molecule colloids like albumin stay in the vessels and pull fluid in.
objectives: You can compare crystalloids and colloids by particle size, where they stay, and what they do.
You can explain what normal saline, lactated Ringer's, and dextrose fluids do.
You can explain how albumin holds fluid in vessels and what low albumin causes.
You can state normal albumin and prealbumin values.
You can monitor a client on IV fluids for fluid overload and anaphylaxis.
You can act first on findings that threaten breathing or circulation.
topics.bigPicture:
IV fluids go straight into a vein, so they enter the blood immediately. That makes them fast and strong. It also means a mistake reaches the client fast. The provider orders the fluid. The nurse must know what it will do, check that it fits the client, and watch the response.

IV fluids come in two main groups. Crystalloids have small particles that move easily between compartments. Colloids have large molecules that stay in the blood vessels and pull fluid in. Learn this difference, plus the role of the protein albumin, and you can predict where any IV fluid goes.
recap: Crystalloids (small particles) spread through the ECF. Colloids (large molecules) stay in the vessels and pull fluid in.
0.9% NS and LR are isotonic. They expand vessel and ECF volume, with no major shift into cells.
Isotonic fluids can cause fluid overload, especially in older adults, and can dilute the hematocrit.
LR has sodium, potassium, calcium, and lactate. Lactate becomes bicarbonate and helps correct metabolic acidosis.
D5W and D5½NS give hydration and a little energy. D5W acts like free water once the sugar is used.
Albumin (5% or 25%) and dextran 40 are colloids, used in shock and burns. Watch for anaphylaxis.
Low albumin causes edema, third spacing, ascites, low blood pressure, and slow wound healing.
Normal albumin is 3.5–5.0 g/dL. Normal prealbumin is 15–36 mg/dL.

keyTerms.def: An IV fluid with small particles, like sodium, chloride, or dextrose, that move easily between compartments. The most common IV fluids.
An IV fluid with large molecules, like proteins, that stay in the vessels and pull fluid into the blood.
Having about the same concentration as blood, so it causes no major shift into or out of cells.
An isotonic crystalloid: sodium chloride in water.
An isotonic, balanced crystalloid with sodium, potassium, calcium, and lactate.
5% dextrose (sugar) in water.
5% dextrose in half-strength (0.45%) saline.
The main protein in plasma. It holds water in the vessels. It is also given as an IV colloid (5% or 25%).
A short-lived protein. It shows recent nutrition, over days. Normal is 15–36 mg/dL.
The water-pulling force of proteins, mainly albumin, in the blood. Also called colloid osmotic pressure.
Fluid that leaves the vessels and gets trapped in tissues or body cavities, where it cannot help circulation.
Fluid collected in the abdomen, a form of third spacing.
The percent of blood volume made of red blood cells.
Blood that is too acidic because of a body chemistry problem, not a breathing problem.
More fluid in the vessels and tissues than the heart and kidneys can handle.
A severe, life-threatening allergic reaction.

sections.heading: What are the two families of IV fluid?
sections.keyIdea: Small-particle crystalloids spread out into the tissues; large-molecule colloids stay in the vessels and pull fluid in.
sections.body:
Every IV fluid is water plus something dissolved in it. What is dissolved, and how big it is, decides where the fluid goes.

Crystalloids have small particles such as sodium, chloride, potassium, and dextrose. These move easily, so the fluid spreads from the vessels into the tissues. Crystalloids are the most common IV fluids.

Colloids have large molecules, such as proteins. They are too big to cross the capillary wall, so they stay in the vessels. There they attract water and pull fluid into the blood from the tissues. For any client, ask: will this be a crystalloid or a colloid?
sections.analogy: Think of the capillary wall as a window screen. Crystalloid particles are like sand. They blow right through, so fluid spreads into the yard (the tissues). Colloids are like tennis balls. They cannot fit through, so they stay in the house (the vessels) and hold water with them.

sections.heading: What do normal saline and LR do?
sections.keyIdea: Isotonic NS and LR fill the vessels and tissues, not the cells, so watch for overload and a diluted hematocrit.
sections.body:
Isotonic fluids have about the same concentration as blood. So there is no major shift into or out of cells. The two to know are 0.9% normal saline (NS) and lactated Ringer's (LR).

They raise vessel and ECF volume, replace sodium, and support circulation. Part stays in the vessels and part moves into the tissues. They do not enter the cells. They are not interchangeable, so match the bag label to the order every time.
bullets: Fluid overload: the biggest risk is a heart or kidneys that cannot keep up. Think older adults, heart failure, and kidney disease. Watch the lungs, weight, and I&O.
Diluted hematocrit: extra fluid adds liquid but no red cells, so the percent drops. This is hemodilution.
Dilution or bleeding? A small drop with stable or improving vital signs suggests dilution. A drop with worsening vital signs suggests bleeding.
Volume is not everything: fluids can fix volume while a lab like potassium stays abnormal. Check every lab.
sections.example: At the bedside: Mrs. W, 79, gets 0.9% NS at 125 mL/hr after days of poor intake. Her hematocrit falls from 42% to 37%. Her vital signs are improving. This is likely dilution, but you still report it and assess for bleeding. Because she is 79, you also check her lungs, breathing, weight, and edema each shift.

sections.heading: What makes lactated Ringer's special?
sections.keyIdea: LR's lactate is turned into bicarbonate, which helps correct metabolic acidosis.
sections.body:
Normal saline has only sodium and chloride. LR is a balanced electrolyte solution. It has sodium, potassium, calcium, and lactate in amounts close to plasma.

The special part is lactate. The liver turns lactate into bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻). Bicarbonate is a base that neutralizes acid. So LR helps correct metabolic acidosis, which means blood that is too acidic from a body chemistry problem, not a breathing problem.

Need volume plus help with acidosis? Think LR. It is working when volume signs improve and bicarbonate and pH move toward normal.
steps: LR goes into the vein.
Lactate travels to the liver.
The liver turns lactate into bicarbonate.
Bicarbonate buffers extra acid in the blood.
Blood pH moves back toward normal.

check.q: Which part of LR helps correct metabolic acidosis, and how?
check.a: Lactate. The liver turns it into bicarbonate, a base that neutralizes extra acid.

sections.heading: What do dextrose fluids do?
sections.keyIdea: Dextrose fluids give hydration plus a little energy, not nutrition; D5W then acts like plain water.
sections.body:
Dextrose is sugar (glucose). Your slides list D5W and D5½NS for hydration and energy support. Read the names like a recipe. D5 means 5% dextrose, or 5 grams of sugar per 100 mL. W means water. ½NS means half-strength saline (0.45%).

The sugar gives a few calories, far too few for nutrition. Cells use it fast. What is left is the water and any salt. So D5W acts like plain water and spreads into all compartments, including cells. That makes it a poor volume expander. D5½NS acts like half-strength saline.

Books label these differently. D5W is often called isotonic in the bag but acts hypotonic in the body. Follow your course materials.

table.caption: Common crystalloids on your slides
rows: Isotonic; raises vessel and ECF volume, replaces sodium, supports circulation
Isotonic and balanced; lactate becomes bicarbonate to help correct metabolic acidosis
Hydration plus energy; acts like free water once sugar is used
Hydration plus energy; acts like half-strength saline once sugar is used

sections.example: At the bedside: Mr. C, 52, is NPO (nothing by mouth) before surgery. He has an order for D5½NS. The dextrose gives some energy while the fluid keeps him hydrated. You watch his blood glucose, especially if he has diabetes. You count the volume as intake and watch for overload.

sections.heading: What are colloids, and when are they used?
sections.keyIdea: Albumin and dextran 40 stay in the vessels and pull fluid in; the first minutes are for watching for anaphylaxis.
sections.body:
Colloids have large molecules that stay in the vessels. They pull fluid from the tissues back into the blood. The main one is albumin, 5% or 25%. It is made from human plasma. Tell clients this honestly, and respect their right to decide. Dextran 40 is a man-made colloid that works the same way.

Albumin is used in shock and burns and reduces third spacing. Shock means blood flow to organs is too low. Third spacing is fluid trapped in tissues, where it cannot help circulation.

Timing for burns: in the first 24 hours, capillaries leak so much that even albumin escapes. So isotonic crystalloid, usually LR, comes first. Albumin is usually added after 24 hours.
bullets: Get baseline vital signs, lung sounds, and weight before you start.
Watch closely in the first minutes for anaphylaxis.
Watch for fluid overload, because colloids pull fluid into the vessels.
Albumin is working when blood pressure rises, urine increases, and edema shrinks.
sections.analogy: A colloid in the blood is like a sponge dropped in a puddle. It stays where you put it and soaks up the water around it.

check.q: Why might a provider order albumin instead of more crystalloid for a client with leaking tissues?
check.a: Albumin stays in the vessels and pulls fluid back from the tissues, raising blood volume. Crystalloids spread into the tissues. For major burns, though, LR comes first in the first 24 hours.

sections.heading: Why does albumin matter so much?
sections.keyIdea: Albumin is a magnet that holds fluid in the vessels; low albumin lets fluid leak into tissues and drops blood pressure.
sections.body:
Albumin is not only an IV fluid. It is the body's main plasma protein, made by the liver. It acts like a magnet for water. It pulls fluid into the vessels, helps keep blood volume, and creates oncotic pressure. In short, albumin keeps fluid inside the blood vessels.

When albumin is low, the magnet is weak. Fluid leaves the blood and moves into tissues. So swollen tissues can sit beside an empty vascular space. The findings are in the bullets.

Low albumin becomes urgent when blood pressure falls. Prealbumin shows recent nutrition over days. Albumin shows longer-term protein status.
bullets: Edema: swelling from fluid in the tissues.
Third spacing: fluid trapped where circulation cannot use it.
Ascites: fluid in the abdomen.
Low blood pressure: less fluid stays in the vessels.
Slow wound healing: swollen tissue and low protein slow repair.

table.caption: Normal lab values
rows: Main plasma protein; oncotic pressure and longer-term protein status
Short-lived protein; recent nutrition (changes within days)

sections.example: At the bedside: Mr. N, 67, has eaten little for weeks. His albumin is 2.4 g/dL. His ankles are swollen, his belly is full of fluid, his blood pressure is low, and a shin wound will not heal. One cause explains it all. You report the lab value and findings.

sections.heading: How do I monitor IV fluids?
sections.keyIdea: Check the order, get a baseline, monitor closely, and judge the fluid by the client's response.
sections.body:
Use these steps each time you hang or monitor an IV fluid. Judge a fluid bolus by the client's response, especially urine output of at least 0.5 mL/kg/hr.

AP can measure and record I&O and report numbers. The nurse assesses, teaches, and interprets. Count the IV fluid as intake.
steps: Check the order: fluid type, volume, and rate. Match the bag label to the order.
Know what it does: crystalloid or colloid? Isotonic? Dextrose?
Get a baseline: vital signs, weight, lung sounds, edema, I&O, and labs such as hematocrit, sodium, and albumin.

Monitor: record all intake and output. Watch for overload: new crackles, shortness of breath, rising blood pressure, fast weight gain, more edema. With colloids, watch for anaphylaxis, especially early.
Evaluate: is fluid status improving? Report abnormal findings to the provider.

sections.heading: What if overload or a reaction starts?
sections.keyIdea: Overload: sit the client up and slow the fluid. Allergic signs on a colloid: stop the infusion first.
sections.body: Two problems need fast action. Know the first move for each. A new breathing problem comes before routine tasks, like a supply request or an expected IV site change.

table.caption: Two IV emergencies
rows: New crackles, shortness of breath, fast weight gain, rising BP, more edema
Itching, hives, hoarseness, wheezing, throat tightness, sudden BP drop
Raise the head of the bed; slow the infusion per policy
Stay with the client, call for help, notify the provider now

sections.example: At the bedside: Mr. R, 81, has heart failure and is getting NS. He gained 1.5 kg overnight and now has crackles. You raise the head of the bed, slow the fluid per policy, assess, and call the provider. If a fast fluid rate is ordered for a client like him, clarify it before starting.

sections.heading: Common traps: look-alikes to tell apart
sections.keyIdea: Know where each fluid goes: isotonic stays in the ECF, D5W goes everywhere, colloids stay in the vessels.
sections.body: These pairs show up as wrong answers. Use the table to tell them apart.

table.caption: Look-alikes and how to tell them apart
rows: Crystalloids spread into tissues. Colloids stay in vessels and pull fluid in.
Both isotonic. LR adds potassium, calcium, and lactate, which becomes bicarbonate.
D5W acts like free water and enters cells. NS stays in the ECF and expands volume.
Dilution: small Hct drop, stable client. Bleeding: Hct drop with worsening vital signs.
Albumin (3.5–5.0 g/dL) shows long-term status. Prealbumin (15–36 mg/dL) shows recent days.
Albumin early vs late in burns
First 24 hours: crystalloid (usually LR). Albumin is usually added after that.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Expect matching fluids to goals, spotting overload or anaphylaxis, and choosing which client to see first.
sections.body: Common question patterns:
bullets: Which fluid fits this goal? Volume, acidosis help, or hydration with a little energy.
Which finding during an infusion needs action first?
Is this hematocrit drop dilution or bleeding?
Which client should the nurse see first?
steps: Read the stem: “A client is receiving 25% albumin. Ten minutes in, the client reports itching and a hoarse voice. What is the nurse's first action?” A) Slow the infusion. B) Stop the infusion. C) Give an antihistamine. D) Recheck vital signs in 15 minutes.
What is it really asking? What is the first move for a possible allergic reaction to a colloid?
Key cues: colloid, early in the infusion, itching, and hoarseness, which hints at airway swelling.
Why the others are wrong: A keeps giving the cause. C needs an order and does not stop exposure. D delays care.
The answer: B. Stop the infusion, stay with the client, call for help, and notify the provider.

check.q: Reusable strategy for IV fluid questions?
check.a: Name the fluid's family and where it goes. Then ask what could go wrong: overload or a reaction. Act first on anything that threatens breathing or circulation.

sections.heading: Worked case: albumin for low blood pressure
sections.keyIdea: Albumin working means blood pressure up, urine up, edema down; new crackles mean overload.
sections.body: Ms. T, 60, has liver disease. Her albumin is 2.1 g/dL. She has ascites, leg edema, and a blood pressure of 90/54. The provider orders 25% albumin.
steps: Why is she sick? Low albumin means weak pull, so fluid leaks into her belly and legs.
Why albumin? It stays in the vessels and pulls fluid back in.
Before starting: get baseline vital signs, lung sounds, weight, and I&O.
Early on: watch closely for itching, hives, wheezing, or a BP drop.
Later: look for BP up, urine up, and edema down. Watch for crackles or shortness of breath.

check.q: Two hours later, her BP is 110/68 and urine output has increased, but she has new crackles. What does this mean?
check.a: The albumin raised her blood volume, but she may now have fluid overload. Raise the head of the bed, slow the infusion per policy, assess, and notify the provider.

pearls: Crystalloid means small particles that spread out. Colloid means large molecules that stay in vessels and pull fluid in.
Know the isotonic pair: 0.9% NS and LR. They expand the ECF without a major shift into cells.
A hematocrit drop after big IV volumes may be dilution when the client is stable. If vital signs worsen, think bleeding. Always assess and report.
LR: lactate becomes bicarbonate, which helps correct metabolic acidosis.
Albumin is used in shock and burns and reduces third spacing. The key colloid risk is anaphylaxis.
Overload risk is highest when the heart or kidneys cannot keep up: older adults, heart failure, kidney disease.
redFlags: New crackles, shortness of breath, or fast weight gain during IV fluids: raise the head of the bed, slow the infusion per policy, assess, and notify the provider.
Itching, hives, hoarseness, wheezing, or a sudden BP drop during a colloid: stop the infusion, stay, call for help, and notify the provider.
Hematocrit dropping with worsening vital signs: think bleeding, not dilution, and report right away.

checks.q: An 84-year-old is on 0.9% NS. What complication worries you most, and what do you monitor?
checks.a: Fluid overload, because older adults have less kidney reserve. Monitor lung sounds, breathing, vital signs, daily weight, edema, and I&O.

checks.q: A client in shock gets 25% albumin. How does it raise blood volume?
checks.a: Albumin is a large protein that stays in the vessels. Its oncotic pressure pulls fluid from the tissues into the blood.

checks.q: Which IV fluid has lactate, and why does that matter?
checks.a: Lactated Ringer's. The liver turns lactate into bicarbonate, which helps correct metabolic acidosis.

checks.q: A client's hematocrit drops from 40% to 35% after 3 L of NS. The client's vital signs are stable. What is one likely reason?
checks.a: Hemodilution. The fluid added plasma but no red cells, so the percent fell. Still assess for bleeding and report.

checks.q: A client's prealbumin is 10 mg/dL. What does this suggest?
checks.a: It is below normal (15–36 mg/dL), which suggests poor recent nutrition (protein status).

checks.q: Why is D5W a poor choice to raise blood volume?
checks.a: Once the sugar is used, D5W acts like plain water. It spreads into all compartments, including cells, so little stays in the vessels.
